body: Her back to the door, a woman is doing the washing up at a quarter past seven on a weekday evening, and in the next room her four-year-old is singing. She stops with a plate in her hand to listen, because he is singing confidently and completely in tune, and what he is singing is the jingle from an advert for a price comparison website. He knows all of it, including the part where the voice goes up. Nobody sat him down and taught it, and nobody could tell you which week it went in. She puts the plate on the rack and calls him through for his bath.

That is not a story about advertising. It is a story about how words get inside a child, and the answer is that they get in sideways — in the background, from whatever happened to be playing while nobody was concentrating on anything.

The honest arithmetic is unfriendly, so here it is flatly. A child in a churchgoing family might get an hour a week of explicit teaching from somebody who is not their parent. That is the whole formal provision.

Take the sideways part literally, because it is the entire mechanism. A child does not learn a language by being taught one. They learn it by standing about in a room where it is spoken about things that are not the language — where somebody wants the salt, or is annoyed about the bins. Vocabulary arrives attached to circumstances, which is why it sticks and why nobody remembers acquiring any of it. It is also why a boy of four has a comparison website jingle and not a catechism. The jingle was in the room repeatedly, at a volume nobody would have called listening. The catechism was on a shelf.

This band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 on air. Two frequencies are for children specifically — one for the very youngest and one for the early school years, which are different jobs and do not share a station.

Building those properly costs a great deal in a way that never shows on the surface, because the material has to survive being played a thousand times in a small kitchen without the adult wanting to put a fist through the speaker. An hour a week against everything else a child hears is not a fair contest, and it was never designed to be one — so whatever occupies the background has to be worth occupying it, and most children’s religious music is written as though it will be heard once, by a parent who has agreed in advance to be patient.

Almost every parent knows the arithmetic and feels caught by it, because the obvious inference is that they are not doing enough. That is where the guilt comes in, and it is worth interrupting early, because it is a poor motivator and reliably produces the same thing: an ambitious plan, drawn up on a Sunday evening in a mood, which lasts nine days and then collapses, leaving the family with the original problem plus the memory of failing at it.

The arrangement Scripture describes is nothing like the plan. The teaching happens at home and it happens constantly — sitting in the house, walking by the way, lying down and getting up, a list built to cover the whole day and to include the parts of it nobody would ever call teaching. The gathering was reinforcement. It was never the delivery mechanism, and a household that treats it as one has mistaken the echo for the voice.
Which changes what a parent is being asked for, and changes it towards relief rather than more work.

Be fair to the alternative before dismissing it. There is a great deal of genuinely good children’s material on screens now, far better than most of what existed a generation ago, and a tired parent who puts it on has done nothing wrong. But a screen takes a child out of the room. That is not a moral complaint, it is a description: what is learned from it is learned alone, facing away, in a posture that cannot include anybody else. Audio leaves the child where they are. It plays into the room rather than out of it, so it can be interrupted, sung over and asked about, and everything a child learns while somebody else is in earshot arrives attached to that person.
Children do not learn what you present. They learn what they overhear.

It is a Thursday in February and a boy of nine is standing in the second row at his grandfather’s funeral, holding a service sheet. The hymn starts and he does not look at the sheet, because he already knows this one. He could not tell you where from. His mother, who has not managed the first verse, hears him beside her and finds she can manage the second. Nobody taught that boy that hymn. It was on in the kitchen for two years when he was small, at a volume nobody would have called listening, while he did jigsaws and argued about carrots.

The words were in the room before he had any use for them, and they were there when he did. That is the mechanism, and it runs one way only: things can only be waiting for a child if somebody put them there years before anybody could see the point.

It would be dishonest to leave that scene on its own, so here is the other half. A station cannot raise anybody’s children. No quantity of good audio compensates for a house where the thing is never discussed, and a family that outsources the words to a speaker will produce children who know them and have never seen them cost anybody anything. Worse: there is no method here at all. Plenty of children have grown up with all the words and left anyway, and some had parents who did everything well and in the right order. Any ministry implying otherwise is trading on your fear.

But that is precisely the reason to stop engineering the outcome and do the small ordinary thing instead. If it could be purchased, the price would be a syllabus, an hour a day and a permanent low-grade guilt, and every parent would have to pay or admit they had chosen not to. Since it cannot, what is left is the part that was always yours and is genuinely doable: be a person your children can watch, and let what you think be audible in the house on a Wednesday rather than reserved for Sundays. Most of what transfers is caught rather than taught, which is either the most reassuring sentence here or the most alarming.

So the answer to the title question is: you, mostly, and not by teaching. That is good news rather than a heavier burden, because it converts an impossible curriculum into an ordinary house with the right things audible in it. Some of it can be shared out, and here is the modest claim a station may make. It cannot raise a child. It can put the words in the room often enough, over enough ordinary Tuesdays, that they are already familiar on the day the child has something to use them for.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Music, which is most of the band — worship, hymns, gospel, country, ambient and much besides. Teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened rather than sung. Family programming, playable in a room with children in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them, 40 across 29 languages. For the school years there is HM 361.90, Jubilee Kids Party, built for six to eight and considerably louder than anything here has implied.

But if you want somewhere to start, start at HM 360.30 — God’s Little Lambs. It is Bible songs and instrumentals for the youngest listeners, three to five, deliberately warm rather than frantic, because it was made on the assumption that a parent would be in the room and would have to be there again tomorrow. The reason to name this frequency rather than another is that it is designed to be on rather than watched. It does not want the child to face it. A good part of it is instrumental, so it can run through breakfast and the twenty minutes before bath when nobody has patience for anything, and the words that do arrive are small words in ordinary sentences with nothing left out because it was uncomfortable. That is what you want in the background of a four-year-old, because the background is where it goes.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies families reach for and when — which is how the next children’s station gets built for the right age.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer, and a very small one. Do not begin a programme. Put HM 360.30 on tomorrow while the toast is on, then get on with the morning and forget about it. You will not be teaching anybody anything, and that is the point — you will be putting some words in a room that already has words in it, and letting them sit there for two years, at a volume nobody would call listening, for a Thursday in February a very long way off.
